To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

we identified a disease-defining WWTR1/Camta1 fusion transcript in epithelioid haemangioendotheloma (EHE) and that this fusion is present in almost all EHEs but absent in other vascular neoplastic diseases.

the t(1:3)(p36q25) translocation in epithelioid haemangioendothelium (EHE) is a disease-defining event that fuses the WWTR1 gene to CAMTA1, which results in inappropriate expression of the CAMTA1 gene in EHE.
we have identified WWTR1/Camta1 gene fusion as the disease-defining genetic event in EHE, a vascular sarcoma.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the discovery of the genetic basis of EHE, a rare and diagnostically challenging sarcoma, and the development of a molecular diagnostic assay that can be used to confirm this diagnosis.
the molecular characterization of a rare tumor,
the identification of disease-defining genetic changes and how they may lead to the development of targeted therapies.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
WWTR1-CAMTA1 gene rearrangement, which is present in virtually every EHE, is a disease-defining event that may serve as a therapeutic target for this vascular sarcoma.
the WWTR1/CAPMTA1 fusion gene is the molecular signature for EHE.
the t(1,3)(p36,q25) chromosomal rearrangement, which results in the WWTR1/CATMA1 fusion gene, is the first disease-defining genetic change in epithelioid sarcoma.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
we have identified a disease-defining translocation in a sarcoma and have shown that it encodes a chimeric transcriptional activator that is specific to this tumor.
we identified a disease-defining fusion gene in EHE, and that the gene fusion encodes a putatively oncogenic fusion protein.
the WWTR1/Camta1 fusion is a disease defining genetic change in epithelioid Hemangioendotheloma.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the use of high-resolution next-generation sequencing approaches can be used to identify the genetic basis of disease in rare cancers.
gene fusions can occur in nonlymphoid malignancies, including sarcomas, and can provide a disease-defining diagnostic and therapeutic target.
gene fusions can be identified using RNA sequencing data, even when the fusion is not detectable by other methods such as RT-PCR.
